title: Dongshan Liangjie
speaker: Junka Ken Oates
summary: Junka Ken Oates introduces Dongshan Liangjie, founder of the Chan school that became Soto, after the sangha chants the Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, a chant attributed to him. Junka traces his life from the child who touched his own face while reading the Heart Sutra, through the awakening with Yunyan over non-sentient beings expounding the Dharma, to the poem written after he glimpsed his reflection in a stream. Junka reads his exchange with a monk about the bird path, which Dogen echoes in the Sansuiko, and his deathbed "delusion banquet." Junka ends with scholars' view that the chant dates from the late twelfth century, young enough when Dogen heard it to come in paperback rather than hardcover.
topics: Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi

sentences.text: So our new directive is to have our dharma talks be about our ancestors for the foreseeable future.
Good morning.
Today I would like to start our dharma talk with a chant, which is why we had you pick up chant books.
If you would turn to page 29, we will find the Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi.
This chant is also known as the Song of the Precious Mirror Samadhi.
In Japanese it is known as the Hokkyozanmai, and its authorship, as you can see, is attributed to Dongshan Liangzhe, or as the Japanese would say, Tozan Ryukai.
I think we should go ahead and chant this before the talk, since that is who we are going to be talking about today.
Song of the Jewel Mirror Samadhi.
*The teaching of thusness has been intimately communicated by buddhas and ancestors.
Now you have it, so keep it well.
Filling a silver bowl with snow, hiding a heron in the moonlight: taken as similar, they're not the same; when you mix them, you know where they are.
The meaning is not in the words, yet it responds to the inquiring impulse.
Move and you are trapped, miss and you fall into doubt and vacillation.
Turning away and touching are both wrong, word is like a massive fire.
Just to depict it in literary form is to stain it with defilement.
It is bright just at midnight, it doesn't appear at dawn.
It acts as a guide for all beings,*
*but it just removes all pains.
Although it is not fabricated, it is not without speech.
It is like facing a jewel mirror: form an image, behold each other.
You are not it, in truth it is you.
Like a babe in the world, in five aspects complete, it does not go or come, not rise nor stand.
Baba Wawa, is there anything said or not?
Ultimately it does not apprehend anything, because its speech is not yet correct.
It is like the six lines of the illumination hexagram: relative and ultimate interact, piled up they make three, the complete transformation makes five.
It is like the taste of the five flavored herb, like a diamond thunderbolt.
Subtly included within the true, inquiry and response come up together,*
*communing with the source, travel the pathways, embrace the territory and treasure the road.
Respecting this is fortunate, do not neglect it.
Naturally real yet inconceivable, it is not within the province of delusion or enlightenment.
With causal conditions, time and season, quiescently it shines bright.
In its fineness it fits into spacelessness, in its greatness it is utterly beyond location.
A hair's breadth deviation will fail to accord with the proper attunement.
Now there are sudden and gradual, in which teachings and approaches arise.
Once basic approaches are distinguished, then there are guiding rules.
But even though the basis is reached and the approach comprehended, true eternity still flows,*
*outwardly still, [unclear: "wordly"] moving, like a tethered colt, a trapped rat.
The ancient sages pitied them and bestowed upon them the teaching.
According to their delusions they call black as white.
When erroneous imagination ceased, the acquiescent mind realizes itself.
If you want to conform to the ancient way, please observe the sages of former times.
When about to fulfill the way of buddhahood, one gazed at a tree for 10 eons, like a battle scarred tiger, like a horse with shanks gone gray.
Because there is the common, there are jewel pedestals, fine clothing.
Because there is the startlingly different, there are the house cat and [unclear: "cow ye"] with his archer skill could hit a target at a hundred paces, but when arrow points*
*meet head on, what has this to do with the power of skill?
When the wooden man begins to sing, the stone woman gets up dancing.
It's not within reach of feeling or discrimination, how could it admit of consideration in thought?
Ministers serve their lords, children obey their parents.
Not obeying is not filial, and not serving is no help.
Practice secretly, working within, like a fool, like an idiot.
Just to continue in this way is called the host within the host.*
In our service today we dedicated the merit of our practice to our ancestors, and some of our ancestors we call out by name during the ceremony.
The [unclear: "sister veneration"] has a long history in Zen, in part due to the influence of Chinese Confucian thought on Buddhism as it passed through China.
To this day, during ordination ceremonies we receive a chart which gives the official version of our ancestry all the way back to Buddha, so that we know who to venerate.
One of the ancestors that we name in the chant, and one that rightfully gets a lot of attention in this building, is Eihei Dogen, who is known as the founder of Japanese Soto Zen.
But during Dogen's time, at the beginning of what we call the 13th century, who would be on the list?
Certainly Shakyamuni Buddha.
Probably not Maha Prajapati, given the gender politics of the time.
Undoubtedly Bodhidharma would be on the list.
I would submit that one of the names Dogen would have singled out would have been Dongshan.
Earlier I referred to Dogen as the founder of Japanese Soto Zen, and the word "Japanese" in that sentence is important.

Just as I mangled Japanese pronunciation with my particular Canadian-inflected North American English accent, the Japanese mangled pronunciation of Chinese terms, a problem that's made worse by the fact that Chinese is a tonal language and Japanese, like English, is not.
Soto Zen is the mangled Japanese pronunciation of the Chinese term [unclear: "saltung chan"], a Chan Buddhist offshoot school which was founded by Dongshan Liangjie.

So just as we recognize Dogen, a foreigner who lived 800 years before us, as the founder of our sect, I suspect Dogen would have recognized the foreigner who lived 400 years before him as the founder of his sect.
Dongshan was born as [unclear: "yu liang jay"], and I am sure I'm mangling that beyond belief, but he lived between 807 and 869 of the common era, during the Tang dynasty in China.
This was a time of great innovation and change in the teaching of the dharma.
Another monk, who died in roughly 867, just a couple of years before Dongshan, was named Linji Yixuan.
That monk was known for his roar, and his name was mangled by the Japanese into Rinzai, and it is by that name that the Chan Buddhist school offshoot that he founded was called.

The two men were actually contemporaries, and despite their different approaches to practice and eventually the different institutional structures of their schools, there's little evidence to suggest that the rivalry that later developed between the sects occurred during their lifetimes.

Dongshan began his life as a member of an educated elite family in his village in the far east of China, just south of Hangzhou Bay, which is still called Hangzhou Bay and is just south of modern-day Shanghai.
He traveled west into the interior to study after he showed promise studying the dharma with his private tutor.

It was reported that he was a child and they were reading the Heart Sutra, and the tutor and they came with the tutor and they came to the line *There are no eyes, no ears, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind.* And Dongshan felt his own face with his hand and then said to his tutor, "I have eyes, ears, a nose, a tongue and so on, so why does the sutra say they don't exist?"

Apparently this impressed the tutor so much that he felt he was unable to teach him any further, and young Dongshan was sent packing to Wuxi Mountain to study with a Chan master named Mo, and he became a novice monk.
He was about eight to ten at the time.
When he turned 21 he went to Sung Mountain, which is the location of the Shaolin Temple, took the full precepts and entered as a monastic.
He spent a large portion of his early life wandering between various Chan masters and hermits in the Hong Zhu region of China.
During this time he met Nan Shuan and Kui Shan, who, if you've ever read the koan [unclear: "compendiation"], feature prominently in those books.
He began a lifelong investigation into the question of whether non-sentient beings possess Buddha nature.
I have to chuckle here, because during the ceremony at the end of practice period [unclear: "narshu so"] was asked whether a doorknob has Buddha nature, and according to Dongshan the answer is yes.
When he asked this question of Kui Shan, the reply was, "It could never be explained to you by means of the mouth of one born of mother and father."
Dongshan did not feel that was a satisfactory answer and asked for a referral to somebody else who could give him a better answer.
He was sent off to see a man named Tan Sheng of Yun Yan.
As is often the case, the masters become known by where they teach, and so Tan Shan is known as Yunyan.
Yunyan had studied with teachers from both the Mazu and Shitou lines.
To clarify the importance of this: during Tang dynasty China, there were traditionally considered to be five houses of Chan Buddhism.
Two of them, Lin Chi, which became Rinzai, and Yang Chi, which the Japanese pronounce Yogi, trace their name back to Mazu.
Three of them, Saotong, which, as I said, is Soto, one called [unclear: "faian"], and Yun Men, all trace their lines back to Shitou.
So his teacher had studied with both of the people who had given rise to all these major schools.
In later years, during the Song dynasty, the Lin Chi school absorbed everybody except Soto.
When they first met, Dongshan asked Yunyan what sort of person was able to hear the [unclear: "dana"] expounded by non-sentient beings.
Yunyan replied, "Non-sentient beings are able to hear it."
Then Dongshan asked, "Can you hear it, Ho Shang?"
Ho Shang means monk.
Yunyan replied, "If I could hear it, then you would not be able to hear the [unclear: "dana"] that I teach."
Dongshan asked, "Why can't I hear it?"
Yunyan raised his fly whisk and said, "Can you hear it yet?"
Dongshan replied, "No, I can't."
Yunyan's reply to that was, "You can't even hear it when I expound the Dharma.
How do you expect to hear it when a non-sentient being expounds the Dharma?"
Dongshan asked, "In which sutra is it taught that non-sentient beings expound the Dharma?" and Yunyan replied, "Haven't you seen it?
The Amitabha Sutra says it."
It says:
*Water birds, tree groves, all without exception recite the Buddha's name, recite the Dharma.*
Reflecting on this, Dongshan had what is always described as the instant moment of realization, and he composed the gatha:
*How amazing, how amazing, hard to comprehend, that non-sentient beings expound the Dharma.
It simply cannot be heard with the ear, but when sound is heard with the eye, then it is understood.*
So that was his realization poem.
Now, Dongshan is considered to be a Dharma heir of Yunyan, but Yunyan died when Dongshan was just 34, and at this time he had already resumed his pilgrimage to other Buddhist centers.
Much of his Dharma record comes from encounters on the road, at various centers and while he was traveling in between.
He is said to have had a second moment of awakening after he was having doubts about Yunyan's teaching and glimpsed his own face in the water while crossing a stream.
He composed this poem that referred back to his teacher:
*Earnestly seeking without, lest it recede far from you.
Today I am walking alone, everywhere I meet him.
He is now no other than myself, but I am not now him.*
There are other verses that we attribute to Dongshan.
He had a traveling companion for years named Shen Shan.
Shen Shen had picked up a needle to mend his clothes, and Master Dongshan asked, "What are you doing?"
"Mending," answered Shen Shen.
"In what way do you mend?" asked Master Dongshan.
"One stitch is like the next," said Shen Shen. [unclear: "shan dong shen"] said, "We've been traveling together for 20 years and you can still say such a thing.
How can there be such craftiness?"
Shen Shen then asked, "How does the venerable monk mend?" and the reply was, "Just as though the entire earth were spewing flame."
So enlightened.
Yet one time the master was washing his bowls and he saw two birds contending over a frog.
A monk who also saw this asked him, "Why does it come to that?" and the master replied, "It is only for your benefit."
Here is another of his poems:
*Students as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, but none are awakened.
They err by searching for the path in another person's mouth.
If you wish to forget form and not leave any traces, wholeheartedly strive to walk in emptiness.*
Finally, at age 52, he received the blessing of his last master's to open a school of his own, which he did on Dongshan Mountains, hence his name.
You can still go there.
It's in the city called [unclear: "gaon"] in Jiangxi Province.
While at this temple he is said to have gathered between 500 and a thousand followers and to have named 26 Dharma successors.
It is also here that he is said to have composed the song of the [unclear: "jewel mirrors the mirror samadhi"].
He eventually died at age 63, and he is said to have announced the end of his life several days prior to it actually happening.
He told his grieving students that if they felt so bad, they should create a delusion banquet.
At the banquet he took one bite, told his students to, quote, "make a great commotion over nothing," close quote, went to his room and died.

So I'm a bit of a history nerd, and, to have a little bit of a digression in history, I think it's important to contemplate some significant differences between the medieval world and the modern world.
In the modern world we've become very accustomed to the strength of institutions.
Just recently we saw the strength of the institution of a democratic republic overcoming the autocratic tendencies of the leader of a cult of personality.
In medieval times the world over, the autocrat generally won, okay, because institutions were not very strong.
The world in medieval times was much more dependent on the individual leader than on the institution that they led, and it was almost always a he who was doing the leading.

One example of this in European history is Henry the Fifth of England, who through personal leadership and charisma managed to become king of both England and France, only to have his son Henry the Sixth, who ascended to the throne as a child after Henry the Fifth's death, lose the French throne.
There was no robust English institution to keep a hold of the French crown, only the strength of the individual king.

So while Asian societies, and especially China, were significantly ahead of Europe on the scale of robustness as far as institutions went, they were still nowhere near the strength and complexity of modern era institutions.
The five schools that I mentioned of the Tang dynasty era weren't really sects the way that we characterize them now.
They were basically groups of students who had gathered around particularly charismatic and skillful teachers, and Dongshan was one of these teachers.
The fact that he was a popular and prolific teacher meant that he left enough followers to provide the critical mass to form a separate sect.

It also made it more likely that enough of those followers possessed the organizational skills necessary to create a robust institutional structure, allowing the [unclear: "sector percent"] to persist today, which is more than 11 and a half centuries after he died.
Because of all of this, Dongshan's legacy was still strong at the time of Dogen.
Dogen wrote Sansuiko, which you may recognize as the name of the temple here, the Mountains and Water Sutra.
Dogen wrote that, and this is from Sansuiko:
*The stone woman gives birth to a child in the night.*
Modern author Shohaku Okumura points out in his excellent commentary on the Sansuiko kyo that this is a reference to the [unclear: "hokios"] that we just chanted, where Dongshan wrote that
*the wooden man starts to sing, the stone woman gets up dancing.
It's not reached by feelings for consciousness, how could it involve the liberation?*
So Dogen was calling back to that 400 years after Dongshan's death.
Also in Sansuiko, Dogen wrote:
*However many great sages and wise men we suppose have assembled in the mountains, ever since they entered the mountains no one has met a single one of them.
There is only the expression of the mountain way of life.
Not a single trace of their having entered remains.*
In his analysis, Shohaku Okumura notes that this refers to Dongshan's discussion of what was called the bird path.
Okumura points out that migratory birds know where they're going every year, but humans can't see the path they follow.
Although we don't see their flyway, the birds know it.
Even though the traces don't last, the masters are like birds with no trace we can see.
Nonetheless, the birds can find the path.
If we love the mountain's way of life, even without footprints, still we see the traces of the masters' way of life.
And this all relates back to the following exchange between Dongshan and one of his monks.
*The monk said, "The master normally tells us to follow the bird path.
I wonder what the bird path is."
"One does not encounter a single person," replied the master.
"How does one follow such a path?" asked the monk.
"One should go without hemp sandals on one's feet," replied the master.
"If one follows the bird path, isn't that seeing one's original face?" said the monk.
"Why do you turn things upside down?" asked the master.
"But where have I turned things upside down?" asked the monk.
"If you hadn't turned things upside down, then why do you regard the slave as the master?" said the master.
"What is one's original face?" asked the monk.
"Not to follow the bird path," answered Dongshan.*
I just love how opaque this stuff gets.
I was writing this talk for the better part of a week, trying to contemplate these things.
I am still clueless.

But as the school of [unclear: "satang"] Chan developed, the idea took hold that the use of koans should not have a specific goal, because that would imply a dualistic distinction between ignorance and enlightenment.

This was built on Dongshan's perspective of not basing practice on stages of enlightenment. [unclear: "Satang"] devotees were encouraged to take a self-fulfilling rather than a competitive path to enlightenment.
This is contrasted with Linji's successors, who derided Soto as what they called silent illumination Chan.
In their practice they used koans almost as verbal sparring, and if you've ever read the collections of koans, they really are verbal fighting with the Dharma.
The [unclear: "satang"] concept that one should practice with no gaining idea, as Suzuki Roshi said, persists today in our practice.
There's a lot more about Dongshan we can delve into.
He had a series of verses called the verses of five ranks, but I think it's probably enough without going into that, which would be an entire Dharma talk on its own.
As a final twist, I will share that modern scholars now believe that Dongshan had no personal hand in writing the verse we just chanted.
It was probably written in the late 12th century in a monastery that was of Dongshan's lineage, but it was not actually, in all likelihood, written by Dongshan himself.
That brings up an interesting point, because if it was late 12th century, that means it was probably only a few decades old when Dogen heard it in China.
Old enough that he could have gotten it in paperback instead of hardcover, but not really ancient.
So we can give Dongshan credit, I think, for the ideas that it displays, as the people who wrote it were undoubtedly his followers, but it just goes to show that nothing really is as it seems.
So that is the actual founder of our Soto, all due credit to Dogen, and thank you very much.
